criteria.name: Introduction — Identifies ethical issues and broad links to engineering design; discusses the context of ethical issues in engineering organisations; identifies relevant stakeholders when considering the ethical issues.
criteria.reasoning: The introduction clearly identifies three core ethical issues within engineering design and organisational decision-making. Stakeholder perspectives, interests, and decision authorities are systematically articulated through Table 1.

evidence.quote: Three ethical issues follow. First, test coverage is being set by the release calendar instead of by risk
Second, the rule treats data loss as harmless, which stops being true once the customer is a government health department

criteria.name: Balanced Discussion — Discusses objective arguments for and against decisions on the ethical issues; draws a conclusion on how stakeholders should make decisions about the issues.
criteria.reasoning: The report presents a balanced and thorough discussion, examining both commercial/learning benefits of shipping and public safety/liability risks of withholding. Actionable recommendations are provided across multiple stakeholders.

evidence.quote: When the WannaCry ransomware made data unavailable in the National Health Service in May 2017, no medical device malfunctioned
Rachel should withhold quality sign-off for the health contract, record the untested failure modes in writing and escalate to management.

criteria.name: Compelling Argument that supports conclusion — The report forms a compelling argument that justifies the conclusion; the body follows a logical structure, with linked paragraphs and content ordered to support the argument; arguments demonstrate a systematic understanding of the ethical issues for all stakeholders.
criteria.reasoning: The report builds a logically rigorous and compelling argument. It moves systematically from problem context to comparative options analysis in Table 2, supporting justified conclusions and recommendations.

evidence.quote: Options B and C respect every stakeholder's interests better than either extreme. They keep most of the commercial benefit

criteria.name: Research and Evidence — Arguments are substantiated with adequate references and qualitative/quantitative evidence; research demonstrates a balanced, in-depth understanding of the topic.
criteria.reasoning: Arguments are substantiated with qualitative analysis, quantitative data, and four distinct case studies (WannaCry, Therac-25, Pentium, VW), alongside professional codes and risk standards.

evidence.quote: Intel found the Pentium division flaw in 1994, judged it too rare to matter and kept shipping

criteria.name: Report Structure, Format and Language — The report includes appropriate sections serving their functions (abstract, introduction, body, and conclusion); maps, figures, tables, and visual elements are correctly used to support discussion; writing is grammatically correct, fluent, concise, easy to read and understand, and uses appropriate word choice; references are well-structured and appropriate, supporting the report’s motivations.
criteria.reasoning: The report exhibits excellent structure, concise writing, flawless language, and professional IEEE referencing. Tables and a flowchart visual element (Figure 1) are competently deployed.

evidence.where: How should Rachel decide when to ship?

requirements.where: How should Rachel decide when to ship?

overall: An exemplary report demonstrating rigorous ethical reasoning, effective integration of case studies and standards, and a practical risk-based decision framework tailored to engineering practice.

feedback.summary: You have produced an outstanding report that achieved top marks across all criteria. Your analysis demonstrates exceptional depth, combining clear stakeholder identification in Table 1, objective trade-off evaluation, and thorough grounding with external cases like WannaCry and Therac-25. The inclusion of Figure 1 and structured decision matrices made your recommendations both practical and compelling. To maintain this standard, continue bringing this level of rigorous risk modelling and visual synthesis to professional engineering scenarios.
next_steps: Adapt your Figure 1 decision flowchart into a standardized risk matrix framework for use in other complex engineering design projects.
Continue to reference formal safety and governance standards alongside historical case studies when justifying engineering trade-offs.
Explore implementing quantitative cost-benefit models to further reinforce stakeholder trade-off analyses in future reports.

criteria.C1: You clearly introduced three ethical issues linked to engineering design constraints and release pressures in the INTRODUCTION. Your use of Table 1 systematically mapped stakeholder interests and decision authorities. To maintain this Excellent standard in future engineering reports, continue defining stakeholder risk appetites and organisational power dynamics as early and explicitly as you did here.
criteria.C2: In Arguments for shipping and Arguments against shipping, you provided a balanced, objective evaluation balancing commercial timelines against public safety. Your actionable conclusions in RECOMMENDATIONS effectively addressed distinct roles, including Rachel and management. To sustain this Excellent standard, continue detailing how conflicting stakeholder mandates can be reconciled through operational compromise.
criteria.C3: Your report builds an exceptionally compelling argument that naturally leads to your conclusions. In The Most Ethical Path and Table 2, your comparative options analysis systematically resolved competing stakeholder needs rather than resorting to binary choices. Maintain this standard by continuing to guide readers through structured trade-off matrices before delivering final recommendations.
criteria.C4: You substantiated your claims thoroughly using both qualitative arguments and quantitative standards, integrating relevant case studies like Therac-25, WannaCry, and the Intel Pentium flaw. To keep achieving at this Excellent level, ensure future work continues to ground historical precedent directly into specific technical risk models.
criteria.C5: Your writing is fluent, concise, and structured logically throughout. Visual aids, particularly the decision flowchart in Figure 1 and structured tables, effectively reinforced your methodology alongside accurate IEEE referencing. To preserve this Excellent rubric level in future professional reports, continue using process flowcharts to synthesize complex procedural decision paths.
